description: Evidence-graded catalog of external tools and platforms used across the GenAI career lifecycle: one record per tool or tightly defined tool class, with what it does, a verdict from the rubric, the evidence behind the verdict, its grade, a line-level session citation and the date the evidence was retrieved. 'stage' uses the repository's folder numbers: 0 cross-stage, 1 landscape, 2 roles, 3 skills, 4 certifications, 5 portfolio, 6 job search, 7 networking, 8 interviewing, 9 compensation, 10 onboarding, 11 tracks.
basis: Built from the tool catalogs, findings and operating rules of the October 2026 research sessions. The main source is T0-10, the 12-stage tooling audit (retrieved 2026-10-21); T0-04, T0-05, T0-11, T0-13, T0-14, T0-02, T0-17, T0-07, T0-18, T0-06, T0-09, T0-08 and T1-03 add the tools of their domains. No tool was tested hands-on: verdicts rest on vendor documentation, pricing pages, reviews, datasets and studies as each session graded them, so no verdict validates outcomes. Verdicts follow the sessions. T0-10 Recommended maps to use, Viable to use-with-care and Avoid to avoid. T0-10 Caution maps to use-with-care when the session names a safe use or control, to watch when the blocker is newness or unverified status, and to avoid where the sessions' operating rules say not to rely on it: products whose core function is auto-applying (rejected by T0-04 R6 and T0-10.F4) and LLM career or salary advice. Explicit 'skip' or 'avoid' verdicts in T0-05 and T0-18 also map to avoid. Where sessions conflict, the record says so and takes the more cautious verdict. 'evidence' is the weakest grade among the claims in 'why', on the cited session's own A-D scale (A primary or measured, B transparent secondary, C vendor, third-party or single-source, D recall or judgement); C and D claims are attributed in the text. 'as_of' is the earliest retrieval date among the cited sources; re-verify statuses and prices within 90 days of it. Out of scope by design: communities, including Blind (career/07-networking/communities-guide.md); credentials themselves, including T0-10's certification rows, and engineering frameworks (both in data/skills_ontology.json); and employer-side systems that candidates do not choose (ATSs, AI screening layers, engineering-analytics tools). Beyz and Interviews by AI are omitted because T0-10 found no evidence about them (grade E). Records apply research/ERRATA.md U13, U16 and U17. Tax, visa and legal entries are pointers, not advice.

rubric.use: Default choice for its job. The session recommends it, or it is the official or primary source for that job, and no documented data, billing, terms or stability risk argues against it. Check prices and dates before paying.
rubric.use-with-care: Usable within the control or limit stated in 'why'. Evidence of benefit is thin, vendor-only or unvalidated, or a manageable risk applies (data exposure, billing pattern, platform terms, stability).
rubric.avoid: Do not use for the purpose named. A hard disqualifier applies (a regulator or court finding of deception, a core function that breaches a platform's terms, undisclosed live assistance in an assessed setting, or shutdown without export), or a session explicitly rejects it for that use (for example mass or unattended auto-apply, exam dumps, acting on an LLM's salary number, or paid tooling a session judges unnecessary at job-seeker scale).
rubric.watch: Not assessable yet: new, in beta, changing ownership, or with existence, pricing or behaviour that the sessions could not verify or that conflict, and no safe default use is stated. Do not rely on it; re-check before use.

tools.name: General LLM assistants for drafting and rehearsal (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and similar)
tools.what: Chat assistants used to structure résumé material, draft notes and rehearse interviews or negotiations, with a human checking every claim.
tools.why: In a field experiment with about half a million jobseekers, non-generative writing help raised hires by 8% and wages by 10% (on one online labour market); after an AI cover-letter tool launched on one platform, cover letters became less correlated with hiring. Use it for structure and practice, verify every claim and keep your own voice.

tools.name: General LLM assistants as career or salary adviser
tools.what: Asking a chat assistant which career to choose or what salary to ask for, and acting on its answer.
tools.why: Peer-reviewed work found LLMs recommend different salary asks to different personas given the same facts (earlier models), and career-advice audits found bias. T0-10 rates advisory use Caution and limits LLMs to drafting and rehearsal: never act on an LLM's number, and check any figure against two data sources.

tools.name: BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook
tools.what: US government occupational profiles and employment projections.
tools.why: Official and free; one of four tools that met T0-10's Recommended bar. It is revised every two years, so it likely lags fast AI-driven shifts (T0-10's inference).

tools.name: O*NET OnLine and My Next Move
tools.what: Official US occupation database and interest profiler (My Next Move).
tools.why: Official and free; its data sources cite BLS 2024-34 projections and CareerOneStop updates through March 2026. It met T0-10's Recommended bar, and like the BLS handbook it likely lags fast AI-driven shifts.

tools.name: Huntr Job Search Trends reports
tools.what: Vendor reports on application volume, conversion by source and ATS share, built from Huntr users' self-tracked applications.
tools.why: A large dataset (Q1 2026: 139,927 applications from 25,635 users), but vendor-run, self-tracked and correlational, and its users skew tech. Read its conversion figures for direction, not magnitude.

tools.name: roadmap.sh
tools.what: Free, open-source role and skill roadmaps.
tools.why: Free and open source, but T0-10 rated it viable from recall only (not verified in-session), so there is no evidence on its quality or currency.

tools.name: Coursera (including Udemy after the merger)
tools.what: MOOC and certificate marketplace; Coursera and Udemy completed their merger in May 2026.
tools.why: No ROI evidence was found for any MOOC, and catalogue and pricing may shift after the merger. The one causal study (800,000+ Coursera certificate earners without degrees in developing countries) found that sharing a credential raised employment by 11 points for those induced to share, concentrated among learners with low or moderate baseline employability.
tools.status: merged: Coursera and Udemy, completed May 2026

tools.name: freeCodeCamp
tools.what: Free coding curriculum run by a nonprofit.
tools.why: Free, but T0-10 rated it viable from recall only (not verified in-session), and no ROI evidence was found for any MOOC.

tools.name: Hugging Face Learn
tools.what: Free structured courses on LLMs, agents, MCP and post-training (smol), plus a cookbook.
tools.why: An official, free catalogue; the Agents Course certificate requires Unit 1, a use-case assignment and a final challenge. T0-10 rated it from recall only, and like every MOOC in its audit it has no ROI evidence.

tools.name: Kaggle (Learn courses and notebooks)
tools.what: Free micro-courses and free GPU notebooks for practice and small experiments.
tools.why: Free 16 GB-class GPU notebooks with 12-hour GPU or CPU sessions and 9-hour TPU sessions; the weekly GPU quota often quoted (about 30 hours) was not in the docs T0-06 could see. Kaggle Learn courses are rated from recall only.

tools.name: DeepLearning.AI courses and certificates
tools.what: Short courses and specialisations; certificates are course-completion records with public verification pages.
tools.why: Short courses are free (per a course listing); certificates need a paid Pro membership (about $30–50 a month, sources conflict) and are unproctored completion records. T0-11 rates the certificate Tier 3 as a credential and Tier 2 (situational) as learning for weak-résumé candidates.

tools.name: NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute (DLI)
tools.what: NVIDIA workshops and courses; DLI workshop certificates are separate from the proctored NVIDIA-Certified exams.
tools.why: DLI certificates are earned through a workshop assessment, but the catalogues found date from 2019–2021, so current price and format are unverified. For early-career candidates targeting product companies, T0-11 suggests free NVIDIA course content as learning without paying for a certificate.

tools.name: DataTalks.Club LLM Zoomcamp
tools.what: Free, cohort-style course on retrieval-augmented generation that ends in a portfolio project.
tools.why: Listed as free, ten weeks long and project-based, but known only through a course roundup; no outcome data.

tools.name: Income-share-agreement bootcamps (BloomTech/Lambda School model)
tools.what: Paid bootcamps financed by a share of future income instead of up-front tuition.
tools.why: Hard disqualifier D1: the CFPB's April 2024 consent order found BloomTech misdescribed its income-share agreements as non-loans and inflated placement claims; its last day of instruction is reported as 31 Dec 2025.
tools.status: closed: BloomTech, last day of instruction reported as 31 Dec 2025

tools.name: Modal
tools.what: Serverless CPU and GPU platform billed per second, used for GPU labs and small deployed endpoints.
tools.why: The Starter plan carries $30 of monthly credit; list GPU rates are about $0.59/h (T4), $0.80/h (L4) and $3.95/h (H100), so the credit buys about 7.6 H100-hours. T0-13 suggests it for intermittent GPU demos.

tools.name: RunPod
tools.what: Rented GPU pods billed per minute, for longer experiments than notebooks allow.
tools.why: Per-minute billing and a credits programme of up to $25K (official page), but the official page showed no numeric prices; trackers put an RTX 4090 at about $0.34/h (community) to $0.69/h (secure). Verify live prices.

tools.name: Lambda (lambda.ai)
tools.what: On-demand H100 and A100 instances for serving or fine-tuning labs.
tools.why: The instances page listed H100 SXM at about $3.99–4.29 per GPU-hour and A100 40GB at about $1.99, while other cached snapshots show $2.99–3.29. Snapshots conflict, so verify live.

tools.name: Official certification portals (AWS, Google Cloud, Microsoft Learn, Databricks, NVIDIA)
tools.what: Vendors' own exam pages and guides: fees, formats, validity, recommended experience and retirement notices.
tools.why: The primary source for every exam fact. Check retirement notices before booking: AWS Machine Learning – Specialty had its last exam on 31 Mar 2026, and Azure AI-102 retired on 30 Jun 2026 (successor AI-103, whose exam page carried a beta label).

tools.name: Credly
tools.what: Public badge verification used by AWS and Google Cloud certifications.
tools.why: Public badge links show active or expired status. T0-11 advises listing the full credential name, exam code, issue and expiry dates and a public Credly link on the résumé. Pearson owns Credly and also delivers exams through Pearson VUE.

tools.name: Exam-dump sites
tools.what: Sites selling leaked or reconstructed certification exam questions.
tools.why: Dump material for AWS MLA-C01 is sold openly in 2026, and relying on it destroys the only thing a multiple-choice credential signals. No independent cheating-rate measurement exists for AWS, Google or Microsoft exams.

tools.name: GitHub profile and GitHub Pages
tools.what: Code hosting and a free static site for a portfolio.
tools.why: Rated viable from recall (not verified in-session). Keep source exportable, publish from a domain you own and never commit secrets: platform risk is real, and Read.cv was wound down within months of its acquisition.

tools.name: Hugging Face Spaces
tools.what: Hosting for ML demos: static sites, Gradio and Docker apps, and optional paid GPUs.
tools.why: Static Spaces are free (T0-13's pick when there is no budget, with replay and a recorded walkthrough), but Gradio or Docker Spaces on compute need PRO ($9 a month), apart from up to two ZeroGPU Spaces on free accounts. Free CPU hardware sleeps after about 48 hours idle, and a paid GPU Space bills until paused (a T4 small left on for 30 days is about $288).
tools.status: changed: Gradio and Docker Spaces on compute require a paid plan; older tutorials say they are free

tools.name: Railway
tools.what: App hosting billed per minute of usage.
tools.why: Free plan with a $1 monthly credit; Hobby $5 a month including $5 of usage; Pro $20 a month. T0-13 lists Railway Hobby as an option for a demo budget of up to about $10 a month; free resources are small.

tools.name: Replicate
tools.what: Hosted model APIs, reportedly billed per second.
tools.why: Part of Cloudflare after an acquisition announced in November 2025; product direction may change, and T0-13's demo-platform decision tree does not include it.
tools.status: acquired: by Cloudflare, announced November 2025

tools.name: Read.cv
tools.what: Former professional profile and portfolio site.
tools.why: Hard disqualifier D4: Perplexity acquired it in January 2025 and users had until 16 May 2025 to export. Keep portfolio work on exportable, own-domain hosting.
tools.status: closed: acquired by Perplexity in January 2025; export deadline 16 May 2025

tools.name: GitHub Actions
tools.what: CI and scheduled jobs that re-run a project's tests and evaluation and publish the results.
tools.why: Standard hosted runners stay free for public repositories, and T0-13's CI-gate artifact (tests plus a capped smoke evaluation on every PR, a scheduled full run) lives here. A 2026 charge for self-hosted runners was announced, then postponed (status not re-verified). Give evaluations that call paid APIs a per-run spend cap.

tools.name: Shields.io endpoint badges
tools.what: README badges fed by JSON that a CI run writes.
tools.why: Endpoint JSON needs schemaVersion 1, a label and a message. A badge is only self-asserted (V0) evidence unless it links to the run or file that produced it.

tools.name: OpenAI project spend limits
tools.what: Organisation and project monthly limits on API spend.
tools.why: Turn on 'Enforce a hard limit' so calls fail with HTTP 429 after the limit; a limit without the toggle only sends alerts. Enforcement is not instantaneous, so a public demo also needs its own rate limits and daily budget counter.

tools.name: Anthropic Console workspace spend limits
tools.what: Per-workspace monthly spend and rate limits under the organisation limit.
tools.why: Workspace limits must sit below the organisation limit, and the Default Workspace has no limits, so create a named workspace for each demo or project and cap it.

tools.name: OSS Insight
tools.what: Free analytics over GitHub events: pull-request and issue creators and stargazers by company and geography.
tools.why: Free, with a data explorer and a public API over 5+ billion rows of GitHub event data; T0-05 uses it to choose repos and find the employers that staff them. Employers are inferred from public profile data, so treat company tables as approximate.

tools.name: git log on a treeless clone
tools.what: Local, unmetered count of which employer email domains commit to a repository.
tools.why: T0-05's preferred method for repo research and the basis of its eight-repo contributor statistics. It counts commits, not pull requests, and noreply addresses hide employers. Never turn the output into an email list: GitHub's Acceptable Use Policy bars using it for unsolicited email.

tools.name: GitHub GraphQL API
tools.what: Programmatic access to repository history and contributor data.
tools.why: Free, with 5,000 points an hour per user; research only, because GitHub's Acceptable Use Policy §7 bars using results to send unsolicited email. T0-05's query sketch was untested.

tools.name: Google Jobs and direct employer career pages
tools.what: Search aggregation that leads to applying on the employer's own careers page.
tools.why: The highest source conversion in Huntr's vendor data (7.12%; correlational, user mix varies). Verify recruiters against the official careers page: job and employment-agency scam losses reported to the FTC rose from $90M (2020) to $501M (2024).

tools.name: LinkedIn Jobs and networking (free tier, manual use)
tools.what: Job board and professional network, used by hand.
tools.why: Large reach but low source conversion in Huntr's vendor data (2.94%). Never run automation in a logged-in session: LinkedIn prohibits automation tools and names account restriction as the consequence.
tools.status: under investigation: Texas AG investigation of LinkedIn reported July 2026 (allegations)

tools.name: Wellfound
tools.what: Startup job board, free for candidates.
tools.why: 5.02% source conversion in Huntr's vendor data, behind Google (7.12%) and ahead of Indeed and LinkedIn; correlational, and it depends on user mix.

tools.name: Indeed, Glassdoor and Handshake job boards
tools.what: General and campus job boards.
tools.why: Source conversion of about 3.1–3.4% in Huntr's vendor data, below Google's 7.12% (correlational). Ghost jobs are common: 93% of about 593 self-selected Huntr survey respondents had applied to or suspected one.

tools.name: Jobright.ai
tools.what: AI job matching with an agent feature.
tools.why: All evidence comes from competitor posts (T0-10 Caution), and whether its agent submits applications for you is unverified. T0-10 treats any agent that submits as Caution until you have checked, for the specific ATS, that it works and what it answers on your behalf.
tools.status: unverified: agent behaviour and pricing; competitor sources only

tools.name: Simplify Copilot
tools.what: Browser extension that autofills application forms; you review the answers and click Submit.
tools.why: Autofill with a human submit is T0-10's chosen default. Free, with a paid Simplify+ tier reported at about $19.99 a week by a competitor. It is a browser extension: review its permissions, and pause extensions if Ashby shows its spam error.

tools.name: MyGreenhouse
tools.what: Greenhouse's candidate profile and Quick Apply.
tools.why: Free. You can opt out of Greenhouse's AI match score, which Greenhouse says does not automatically advance or reject anyone, and Greenhouse says candidate information is not shared across employers. The evidence is vendor-only.

tools.name: CLEAR identity verification (employer-initiated, via Greenhouse)
tools.what: Optional ID and selfie verification that some employers trigger inside Greenhouse.
tools.why: Free to the candidate, but complete it only through a link you reached from a known channel: a government ID and a selfie are Tier 3 data in T0-10's upload rules.

tools.name: Huntr (tracker and job clipper)
tools.what: Application tracker with a browser clipper; also offers autofill and a résumé builder.
tools.why: Free tier; logging every submission is one of T0-10's operating rules. The evidence is vendor-only, and none of its features is a parser check.

tools.name: Teal
tools.what: Job tracker plus résumé builder with a keyword match score.
tools.why: Teal+ is reported at about $9 a week or $29 a month in roundups, and one reviewer flags weekly auto-renewal, so check billing. Its match score is a keyword-coverage checklist, not a measurement of any real ATS.

tools.name: Jobscan
tools.what: Résumé-to-posting match-rate scanner with formatting checks.
tools.why: Its match rate is a keyword simulation, and no study links checker scores to real ATS ranking or interview rates. Use it only as a list of gaps against a posting, never as a pass/fail gate. Premium is about $49.95 a month (vendor-stated).

tools.name: Resume Worded
tools.what: Résumé feedback with a score.
tools.why: Known only through third-party comparisons; it is not a replica of any ATS parser, and no validation of checker scores against real ATS output was found. Treat its score as a gap list, not a gate.

tools.name: Rezi
tools.what: Résumé builder with its own ATS score.
tools.why: Its score is internal to Rezi (one roundup notes that no real ATS has a universal score), and the evidence is vendor-only. About $29 a month or $149 lifetime in roundups.

tools.name: Kickresume
tools.what: Résumé builder.
tools.why: Its privacy policy reserves the right to train on anonymised user documents, so upload only Tier 1 data (no home address, date of birth or ID numbers). About EUR 8 a month on annual billing (roundup).

tools.name: Enhancv
tools.what: Design-forward résumé builder.
tools.why: Vendor parser claims conflict on whether its design-heavy layouts parse. Use a single-column template and paste the exported text into a plain-text editor to check reading order. About $24.99 a month.

tools.name: BOLD-family builders (Zety, MyPerfectResume, LiveCareer, Resume Now)
tools.what: Subscription résumé builders from the Bold LLC family.
tools.why: T0-10 Caution: a trial of about $3 reportedly converts to about $24 every four weeks, with cancellation and refund complaints, and LiveCareer exposed more than 5.1M files (mostly résumés). If you use one, read the billing terms, pay with a card that has dispute rights and upload Tier 1 data only.

tools.name: Resume.io
tools.what: Résumé builder sold through a low-cost trial.
tools.why: T0-10 Caution: the low-cost trial converts to a monthly subscription, and there is a trial-to-recurring complaint pattern. Read the terms before paying.

tools.name: Canva résumé templates
tools.what: Design templates exported as PDF.
tools.why: T0-10 Caution: a vendor test reports parse failures from image-based exports, and Canva's help pages do not say whether exported text keeps a text layer. Use it for the copy humans read; send a portal only an export that passes a text-extraction check.

tools.name: Open-source PDF checks (pdffonts, pdftotext, PyMuPDF, pypdf, pdfminer.six, pdfplumber)
tools.what: Free local tools that show what text a parser can pull from your PDF, and in what order.
tools.why: One of T0-04's two defensible pre-submission checks: pdffonts should show no Type 3 fonts and a Unicode map on every row, two extractors should read the file in order, then do a copy-paste test. They probe conversion, where most parse failures start, not any vendor's parser.

tools.name: Greenhouse 'Unsuccessful resume parse' checklist
tools.what: Greenhouse's support article listing the conditions that make résumé parsing fail.
tools.why: A vendor-documented trigger list: files over 2.5 MB, letter-spaced text, graphics, image uploads, complex tables, contact data in headers, footers or text boxes, and column layouts. A failed parse leaves fields empty for manual entry; it is not a rejection.

tools.name: Vendor parser demos (for example Textkernel Extract!)
tools.what: Commercial résumé-parser demos or APIs that show how one parsing engine reads your file.
tools.why: T0-04 names a vendor demo as a defensible check but could not reach one. No Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby or Workday document names its engine, and only Oracle Recruiting Cloud lists a Textkernel integration, so a demo shows one engine, not your target ATS.

tools.name: LazyApply
tools.what: Browser extension that bulk-applies to jobs through job boards.
tools.why: Hard disqualifier D2: LinkedIn's terms prohibit the automation it performs. Trustpilot shows about 2.4/5 on roughly 107 reviews, with wrong answers, off-target applications and refund complaints, and T0-04 R6 rejects mass auto-apply.

tools.name: Simplify Autopilot
tools.what: Auto-submit agent that applies to jobs you selected, using weekly credits.
tools.why: Per a competitor's reading of Simplify's help centre it has no review step, and wrong screening answers are the most frequent failure in auto-apply complaints. T0-10 rates it Caution (beta, no outcome evidence) and T0-04 R6 rejects auto-apply; T0-10 re-audits it if it leaves beta.
tools.status: beta

tools.name: Jobscan Auto Apply
tools.what: Agentic auto-apply add-on reported for Jobscan Premium.
tools.why: Reported but not re-verified, with no outcome evidence; T0-10 rates it Caution and T0-04 R6 rejects auto-apply. Jobscan's scanner has its own record.
tools.status: new: launch reported, not re-verified

tools.name: Hosted cloud auto-apply services (FastApply, LoopCV, JobCopilot, Massive, AIApply)
tools.what: Subscription services whose cloud agents fill in and submit applications for you.
tools.why: Not individually audited; one vendor's own test of eight bots claims only three actually click Submit. Cloud agents likely submit from data-centre IPs, which Greenhouse treats as a high-risk fraud signal (T0-10's inference), and T0-04 R6 rejects mass auto-apply.

tools.name: Sonara (relaunched under BOLD)
tools.what: Cloud auto-apply service.
tools.why: The original service shut down on 1 Feb 2024, and the brand was reportedly relaunched under BOLD, per competitor sources. T0-10 rates it Caution and T0-04 R6 rejects auto-apply.
tools.status: relaunched: original service shut down 1 Feb 2024; brand reportedly relaunched under BOLD

tools.name: Scoutify (alerts and 'Sniper' auto-apply)
tools.what: Job alerts plus a career-site auto-apply mode.
tools.why: The only evidence is the vendor's own blog (T0-10 Caution; about $5, $15 or $25 a week, vendor-stated), and T0-10 relied on that blog for other tools. Its auto-apply mode falls under T0-04 R6, which rejects auto-apply.

tools.name: LinkedIn Premium Career and Sales Navigator
tools.what: Paid LinkedIn tiers with InMail credits and title and tenure search filters.
tools.why: Premium Career is about $39.99 a month (5 InMails); Sales Navigator Core $119.99 (50). No data shows candidate InMail beats an email that carries a work artifact, so buy one month at most, and only for the search filters. A Texas AG investigation concerning Premium marketing was reported in July 2026 (allegation).
tools.status: under investigation: Texas AG investigation reported July 2026 (allegations)

tools.name: Third-party LinkedIn automation (PhantomBuster and similar bots and scraping extensions)
tools.what: Tools that send connection requests or messages, or scrape profiles, on LinkedIn for you.
tools.why: Hard disqualifier D2: LinkedIn prohibits bots and extensions that automate activity and names account restriction as the consequence. T0-05 rates PhantomBuster Avoid: at 30 or fewer contacts a week, automation adds restriction risk with no evidence of benefit.

tools.name: ADPList
tools.what: Free mentorship marketplace (a paid tier exists), used for exploration and networking conversations.
tools.why: Free conversations with mentors, but its statistics are self-published and its counts differ across its own pages, so there is no outcome evidence.

tools.name: MentorCruise
tools.what: Paid subscription mentorship.
tools.why: Price sources conflict, and the evidence comes from competitor comparisons; mentor platforms carry self-published evidence only.

tools.name: Apollo.io
tools.what: Prospect and work-email lookup.
tools.why: The free tier (1,200 email credits a year) covers lookups at 30 or fewer sends a week; verify every address, because finder accuracy runs far below vendor claims. Not in Pin's finder audit; LinkedIn removed Apollo's company page on 2025-03-06.

tools.name: Hunter.io
tools.what: Email finder and verifier by company domain.
tools.why: The free tier of 50 credits a month plus manual verification is enough at job-seeker volume. It was not in Pin's finder audit, so its accuracy is unmeasured.

tools.name: RocketReach
tools.what: Paid contact-lookup service.
tools.why: The lowest find rate (29.8%) in Pin's vendor-run audit of 1.3M lookups, against vendor claims of 90–99%; paid plans start at $329 a year (competitor-reported). T0-05's verdict: skip.

tools.name: Clay
tools.what: Data enrichment and workflow orchestration for go-to-market teams.
tools.why: Built for go-to-market teams, with credit-based pricing (Launch $185 a month on annual billing); T0-05's verdict at 30 or fewer sends a week is skip.

tools.name: Paid email finders (Wiza, ContactOut, Forager)
tools.what: Subscription tools that find work emails for named people.
tools.why: Find rates of 55.2%, 48.2% and 45.9% in Pin's vendor-run audit, against vendor claims of 90–99%. T0-05 finds paid tooling mostly unnecessary at 30 or fewer sends a week, where free tiers plus manual verification are enough.

tools.name: Hello Interview
tools.what: System design, ML system design and AI-coding prep, with company guides and AI-run practice interviews.
tools.why: The best-verifiable option for GenAI and ML system design: Premium $47 for a month, $89 for a year or $299 lifetime (21 Oct 2026), with ML System Design and AI Coding tracks. No prep platform has independent outcome evidence, and human mocks no longer appear on its pricing page.
tools.status: changed: human mock-interview pricing no longer listed; a directory says the programme ended 31 May 2026

tools.name: interviewing.io
tools.what: Anonymous mock interviews with experienced engineers; also publishes company process pages.
tools.why: Community praise for calibration and complaints about cost; its GenAI system-design coverage was not verified. Its Anthropic page reports a one-hour design round run in a shared Google Doc.

tools.name: Aced (formerly Exponent; absorbed Pramp)
tools.what: Courses, peer and coach mock interviews, and company system-design guides.
tools.why: A free tier with limited peer sessions plus paid plans (secondary sources), and Pramp was reportedly absorbed. Its company guides are titled 'Aced (formerly Exponent)'; its GenAI system-design coverage was not verified.
tools.status: renamed: Exponent to Aced

tools.name: ByteByteGo
tools.what: System-design books and courses, including a GenAI system-design title.
tools.why: Paid; the GenAI title is reported only in secondary mentions and was not verified in-session.

tools.name: DesignGurus
tools.what: System-design courses, including 'Grokking the AI System Design Interview', and company process guides.
tools.why: A subscription vendor with a disclosed commercial interest; its AI system-design guide offers a three-family taxonomy of prompts.

tools.name: IGotAnOffer
tools.what: Company system-design guides; also a coaching marketplace.
tools.why: Commercial guides; they list AI-native prompts among reported Anthropic questions (a model evaluation and monitoring system, a prompt caching and retrieval system). Its coaching marketplace is recalled, not verified.

tools.name: Interview question aggregators (PracHub, AceOffer, Dataford, Interview Query)
tools.what: Candidate-reported interview questions pooled by company and role.
tools.why: Useful for frequency: AceOffer's tally of 112 Anthropic design reports puts an inference API (41 reports) first. The tallies are unaudited, and syndication duplicates reports.

tools.name: GenAITrail
tools.what: Free 15-question LLM system-design guide with worked numbers.
tools.why: Free and numeric, but single-author; T0-14 drew on it for its framework, worked numbers, rubric and red flags.

tools.name: LeetCode (including Premium)
tools.what: Algorithm problem bank and contests.
tools.why: The baseline for algorithm rounds, because AI-permitted interview formats are a minority and employer policies vary; its question tags reflect past, not current, loops. Rated from recall (not verified in-session).

tools.name: NeetCode
tools.what: Algorithm roadmap and videos, free plus a Pro tier.
tools.why: Covers algorithms only; rated from recall plus one third-party review that was not re-verified.

tools.name: Google Interview Warmup
tools.what: Free AI interview practice with short question sets.
tools.why: Known from secondary roundups only; an experimental Google product whose longevity is unverified. T0-10 found no independent study showing that AI mock interviews improve real outcomes, so treat it as low-stakes rehearsal.

tools.name: Yoodli and Big Interview
tools.what: AI interview practice with speech and delivery analytics.
tools.why: Rated from recall plus roundup mentions, with no outcome evidence. The main risk is data exposure from recorded audio or video.

tools.name: Final Round AI (mock-interview mode)
tools.what: Subscription AI mock interviews from a vendor that also sells a live interview copilot.
tools.why: T0-10 Caution: Trustpilot shows 3.5/5 on about 250 reviews, with refund, lock-out and latency complaints, and its handling of audio and screen captures is unknown because its primary privacy policy was not retrieved.

tools.name: Final Round AI (live Interview Copilot)
tools.what: Live AI assistance during real interviews.
tools.why: Hard disqualifier D3: undisclosed live assistance in an assessed setting. Amazon reportedly tells recruiters to disqualify candidates found using AI tools; follow each employer's stated AI policy.

tools.name: Overlay interview copilots (Cluely, Interview Coder, Parakeet AI, LeetCode Wizard)
tools.what: Tools marketed as undetectable live assistance during interviews.
tools.why: Hard disqualifier D3: undisclosed live assistance in an assessed setting breaks the stated policies of employers that prohibit AI in interviews and risks disqualification. Disclosed use where an employer explicitly permits it is a different case.

tools.name: Excalidraw
tools.what: Virtual whiteboard used in remote system-design rounds.
tools.why: The most common virtual board in Meta design rounds; Hello Interview advises asking which tool your interviewer uses and practising on it.

tools.name: Mermaid diagrams (in CoderPad)
tools.what: Text-to-diagram syntax reported in an AI-enabled design round.
tools.why: Reported for Meta's AI-enabled design round in CoderPad (spring 2026, an early signal); T0-14's practice stack includes a Mermaid cheat-sheet.

tools.name: LLM memory and KV-cache calculators (InventiveHQ, LMCache, the Modular and BentoML handbook)
tools.what: Browser tools and guides that estimate model weights, KV cache and GPU memory.
tools.why: Good for cross-checking your own back-of-envelope estimates while you practise. They rest on heuristics (an overhead factor, bundled model data), and in the interview room you will have only your own formulas.

tools.name: Disposable VM or container for take-homes and recruiter-supplied code
tools.what: A throwaway environment with no credentials for running code a recruiter sends.
tools.why: Fake-recruiter malware is documented: the 'Contagious Interview' campaign delivers malware through coding tests and has been active since at least December 2022 (Microsoft). One of four tools that met T0-10's Recommended bar.

tools.name: Levels.fyi salary database
tools.what: Crowdsourced total-compensation data by company, level, title and location, with structured exports.
tools.why: The anchor for base and big-tech total comp: T0-02 uses its percentile bands by title and city. New-offer entries annualise grants while existing-employee entries report realised value, so cohorts mix. Not a private-equity valuation tool; check currency and location labels in .md exports, and credit Levels.fyi in derived work.

tools.name: Levels.fyi negotiation coaching
tools.what: Flat-fee negotiation coaching in tiers (Standard, Premium, Leadership).
tools.why: Its client cohort reports median comp improvements of about 21% (mid), 23% (senior) and 24% (staff), but buyers are self-selected and typically hold leverage. Money-back terms vary by package and page version, and outcome claims are unaudited.

tools.name: Rora
tools.what: Negotiation coaching priced as a percentage of the increase.
tools.why: Priced as a percentage of the increase (T1-03 also reports about $2,250+); it shows a high Trustpilot score, and its outcome claims are self-reported.

tools.name: Candor
tools.what: Negotiation coaching and offer structuring.
tools.why: Sources conflict: T0-10 rated it viable on a vendor-described success fee (not re-verified), T1-03 describes a fee plus an upside share from community reviews, and T0-02 searched and located nothing. Outcomes are self-reported.
tools.status: unverified: pricing model and status conflict across sessions

tools.name: Fearless Salary Negotiation (Josh Doody)
tools.what: Negotiation book and flat-fee coaching built on an email-template method.
tools.why: Known through a methodology summary and reader reviews, with no outcome data; T1-03 treats such scripts as starting points to adapt, not rigid formulas.

tools.name: Comprehensive.io
tools.what: Crawler of salary ranges posted on US tech career pages.
tools.why: Cross-check only: posted base ranges are not pay, and only 14% of 43,480 US AI-engineering postings mention equity. No AI-engineer percentile page was found, and its current status rests on secondary sources (the daily-crawl claim dates from 2023).
tools.status: unverified: current status known only from secondary sources

tools.name: US DOL OFLC LCA disclosure files
tools.what: Official quarterly H-1B wage filings by employer, job title and offered wage range.
tools.why: A base-wage floor and a within-employer title comparison, not pay: base only, visa-sponsored roles only, titles such as 'Member of Technical Staff' hide seniority, and some filers set range floors at the legal minimum. Process the raw files yourself.

tools.name: Third-party LCA browsers (Ellis, careery.pro, Visaverge, h1bdata.net, MyVisaJobs)
tools.what: Websites that process DOL H-1B filings into employer and title pages.
tools.why: Cross-check only: methods differ, and one aggregator's two OpenAI pages gave San Francisco medians of $180K and $310K. Treat their output as indicative until the raw DOL file is reproduced.

tools.name: Broad crowdsourced salary sites (Glassdoor, Payscale, Indeed, AmbitionBox)
tools.what: Employee-reported and posting-weighted salary averages for the wider market.
tools.why: A different population from Levels.fyi: India's broad market centres near ₹10–15L for AI engineers, against a Levels.fyi Bengaluru ML Engineer median of ₹44.5L. Use them as a population contrast, not for equity-bearing roles.

tools.name: Recruiter salary guides (Robert Half, Michael Page, Cooper Fitch, Hays)
tools.what: Placement-based or survey salary guides published by recruitment firms.
tools.why: Regional cross-checks only: Robert Half's Zurich page reports placement-based starting base excluding bonus, and Michael Page's UAE figures reached T0-02 only through relays. T0-02 advises against binding decisions on Gulf pay bands until primary data replace them.

tools.name: Pave (published reports)
tools.what: Employer-side compensation platform; candidates see only its published benchmarks.
tools.why: Its published reports give useful norms, such as a 6.5% promoted base raise for AI/ML engineers and about +39% ongoing equity at promotion (vendor data). The platform itself is employer-facing, not candidate-accessible.

tools.name: Carta (startup compensation and equity data, calculators)
tools.what: Cap-table platform that publishes startup compensation, tender-offer, dilution and funding data, with free equity calculators.
tools.why: Its published datasets (tender offers, dilution by round, Series A to B graduation) are primary sources for private-equity questions, but its scenario calculators are not validated against outcomes, and the status of its candidate-facing data programme is unverified.
tools.status: unverified: candidate-facing data programme described in a 2023 post

tools.name: Forge Global (Forge Price)
tools.what: Secondary marketplace that publishes indicative prices for about 200 pre-IPO companies.
tools.why: Secondary pricing is bimodal: median trades sit 3–7% below the last primary round, top AI names trade at or above it, and the 2021 cohort sits at a median of −61%. Use Forge Price as a range, not as a valuation of your options.
tools.status: acquisition agreed: by Schwab in November 2025 for about $660M; closing not verified

tools.name: EquityZen
tools.what: Secondary marketplace for employee and investor shares.
tools.why: Morgan Stanley agreed to acquire it on 29 Oct 2025, and the corpus does not assess its pricing, fees or access terms.
tools.status: acquisition agreed: by Morgan Stanley, 29 Oct 2025

tools.name: Capbase Startup Exit Calculator
tools.what: Free tool that models liquidation preferences, participation and dilution at exit.
tools.why: Supports the scenario modelling T0-10 recommends for private equity, once you have the fully diluted share count, strike price, most recent 409A valuation, last preferred price and preference stack. Known from a product listing (launched April 2026), and no tool's equity values are validated against outcomes.
tools.status: new: launched April 2026

tools.name: Autograph Fair Offer
tools.what: Listed as an algorithmic compensation-range and equity-valuation calculator.
tools.why: Seen only as a product listing, with unvalidated accuracy, and T0-10 searched for a 'FairOffer' and found no authoritative result, so its existence and status are unconfirmed.
tools.status: unverified: existence and status

tools.name: Evidently AI ML and LLM system design database
tools.what: Searchable collection of company case studies on ML and LLM systems.
tools.why: 800 case studies from 150+ companies (last updated 22 Dec 2025); T0-09 uses it to find prior art for a new team's use case.

tools.name: AI Incident Database and OECD AI incidents monitor
tools.what: Searchable repositories of reported AI incidents.
tools.why: Searchable incident text and metadata; T0-09 uses them to build a failure-mode taxonomy for a new hire's risk register.

tools.name: danluu/post-mortems
tools.what: GitHub collection of public postmortems.
tools.why: About 250 visible entries, mostly infrastructure failures with few AI-product cases; a reading list for failure shapes before your first postmortem.

tools.name: Remote (employer of record)
tools.what: Employer-of-record service whose Indian entity employs you while a foreign client directs the work.
tools.why: $599 per employee a month on annual billing or $699 month-to-month (vendor page). Against §44ADA an EOR costs a 22–24% take-home haircut up to ₹75L and is near parity at ₹1.2Cr; its value is statutory benefits and lower misclassification risk, not tax.

tools.name: Deel (employer of record and contractor payments)
tools.what: Employer-of-record, contractor-management and contractor-of-record services.
tools.why: EOR at $599 a month per several independent aggregators (Deel's own page was not fetched); contractor management about $49 and contractor-of-record about $325 a month are reported, and its FX margin is reported at about 0.6–2%.

tools.name: Oyster (employer of record)
tools.what: Employer-of-record service.
tools.why: Mostly reported at $699 a month (a few sources say $599); not verified on the vendor page.

tools.name: Wise Business
tools.what: Multi-currency account for receiving and converting foreign client payments.
tools.why: Free to open, with free local receipt in USD, GBP and EUR and fixed SWIFT receipt fees; T0-18 judges it the main rail for India-based providers. The INR conversion cost is not on the page (a payments vendor says about 2–2.5%), and its RBI cross-border aggregator status is reported inconsistently.

tools.name: Payoneer
tools.what: Cross-border receiving accounts with withdrawal to a local bank.
tools.why: Free receipt into a local-currency account, 1% (minimum $1) into a non-local one, and withdrawal or conversion at 1.2–4%, varying by territory. Payoneer reports in-principle, not final, RBI authorisation as a cross-border payment aggregator; confirm the current status.

tools.name: Skydo
tools.what: India-focused invoicing and collection of foreign payments, with auto-generated FIRA.
tools.why: Its final RBI cross-border aggregator authorisation (January 2026) and auto-generated FIRA are reported only by the vendor and third-party lists; check RBI's list before relying on it.

tools.name: PayPal (for freelance invoices)
tools.what: Consumer and business payments service.
tools.why: About 8–9% payment friction for India-based freelancers, per a payments vendor; T0-18 advises against it for large invoices.

tools.name: Stripe Invoicing
tools.what: Card and bank-debit invoicing.
tools.why: 0.4% (Starter) or 0.5% (Plus) per paid invoice, plus card and bank-debit processing fees charged separately. Prices were read on Stripe's Bulgaria page; a US page was not fetched.

tools.name: Bonsai
tools.what: Contracts, proposals, invoices and time tracking for independents.
tools.why: $15, $25, $39 or $59 per user a month ($9–49 billed yearly); proposals, contracts and invoicing start at the Essentials plan, and processing fees vary by payment method. T0-18 did not review its template wording.

tools.name: GST Portal (India)
tools.what: India's goods and services tax portal for registration, LUT filing, returns and refunds.
tools.why: Registration is mandatory at all four billing levels T0-07 modelled, and zero-rated export invoicing rests on an annual LUT filed here; GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B returns and refunds also run through it. Pointers, not tax advice.

tools.name: Income Tax e-filing portal (India)
tools.what: India's portal for income-tax returns, AIS and TIS statements, advance-tax payments and the foreign-tax-credit form.
tools.why: The official route for ITR-3 or ITR-4 filing and advance tax. T0-07 reports that form numbers changed under the 2025 Act and the 2026 Rules but did not verify the new numbers. Pointers, not tax advice.

tools.name: RBI list of authorised payment aggregators
tools.what: The Reserve Bank of India's list of authorised payment aggregators, including cross-border (PA-CB) entities.
tools.why: The check T0-07 prescribes before you rely on any fintech rail, because every PA-CB status in its catalogue is vendor-reported. T0-07 could not retrieve the current list.

tools.name: Go Fractional
tools.what: Fractional-work job board with profiles and rate tools; handles contracts, invoicing and payouts.
tools.why: Free membership with a $500 referral programme; T0-18 judges it the primary secondary channel for fractional leaders. Its rate benchmarks come from its own survey (n = 213), so treat them as vendor data.

tools.name: Fractional Jobs
tools.what: Fractional job board and sponsor of a large fractional-work survey.
tools.why: Its fees are unverified: the site was blocked to T0-18, and a competitor says it charges no platform fee or markup. Confirm fees and any exclusivity directly before using it as a lead source.

tools.name: Toptal
tools.what: Vetted freelance marketplace.
tools.why: No fee to talent, and you set your own rate, but the client markup is undisclosed (estimates 30–50%), and contracts reportedly bar working directly with Toptal-sourced clients (competitor page; the official FAQ is silent). Read the terms.

tools.name: Braintrust
tools.what: Talent network for freelance engagements.
tools.why: 0% talent fee and 100% of earnings on clients you bring. Directories disagree on the client-side fee (10–15%) and report a 15% conversion fee if a client hires you full-time within six months; the official FAQ gave no fee information.

tools.name: Catalant
tools.what: Expert marketplace for enterprise consulting projects.
tools.why: T0-18 judges it a fit for senior consultants with enterprise-project credentials: winning experts typically have 10–20 years' experience and are paid whether or not the client pays Catalant. Its fee is reported at 20–30% of total fees (about a 25–43% markup), with no official figure.

tools.name: Contra
tools.what: Commission-free freelancer platform for portfolios and direct invoicing.
tools.why: 0% commission, a free tier and Pro at about $29 a month or $199 a year, per secondary sources (its pricing page was blocked); some payment fees apply to free-plan transactions.

tools.name: Upwork
tools.what: Bidding marketplace for freelance contracts.
tools.why: A 0–15% freelancer fee, shown before the proposal and fixed per contract (vendor). T0-18 judges it a utilisation filler only, because of commodity pricing pressure; its rate evidence is mixed (per-contract earnings down 13%, AI work up 34% an hour).

tools.name: Fiverr
tools.what: Commodity freelance marketplace.
tools.why: It lists AI strategy consultants at $10–125 an hour and AI agent builds at about $295 a project; T0-18 judges it not suitable for senior work.

tools.name: Common Paper standard agreements
tools.what: Free CC BY 4.0 contract standards: a Professional Services Agreement (v1.1), NDAs and an AI Addendum (v1.0).
tools.why: T0-18's base template; its services agreement sets general and increased liability caps on the cover page. The AI Addendum covers data usage, training rights, IP and liability, but its clause text was not retrieved. Have AI, IP and liability terms reviewed by a lawyer.

tools.name: Bonterms Professional Services Agreement
tools.what: Open standard contract terms.
tools.why: The v1.2 cover page lets you choose licensed or assigned deliverables, but its licence is shown as both CC BY 4.0 and CC0, and the standard terms were not retrieved. Verify before use.

tools.name: OpenAgreements
tools.what: Free library of 125 contract templates, including Common Paper's.
tools.why: Good for browsing and comparing templates; each template keeps its source licence, and the site calls itself legal research, not legal advice.

tools.name: Freelancers Union Contract Creator
tools.what: Free beta generator for contracts covering scope, payment terms and deadlines.
tools.why: No IP clause is mentioned, so it is too thin for AI work: in India a contractor is the first owner of the code, and an assignment silent on duration and territory defaults to five years and India only.

tools.name: Immigration petition providers (Deel Immigration/Legalpad, Manifest Law, Beyond Border Global, WeGreened/NAILG, VisaNation, Tukki, Alma)
tools.what: Firms that prepare US O-1 and EB-1 petitions or screen eligibility.
tools.why: Approval claims are self-reported (for example '98% approval' and '91% success under approval-or-refund'), and no independent audit of any provider's approval rate was found. Published fees include $6,999 to $12,500 (Manifest Law) and about $8k for an O-1 (Beyond Border Global); free eligibility screens exist. Pointers, not legal advice.

tools.name: Official immigration portals (USCIS, GOV.UK, Canada ESDC and IRCC, Singapore MOM, France-Visas, UAE)
tools.what: Government pages for criteria, fees and steps, plus official tools such as Canada's Job Bank wage search and Singapore's EP self-assessment tool.
tools.why: The primary sources behind every visa fact; provider pages and success stories are self-reported. T0-08 lists several items likely to change within six months, so re-read the official page on the day you act. Pointers, not legal advice.
